title: Mean Time to Detect and Respond
shortTitle: Mean Time to Detect and Respond
summary: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) is the average elapsed time between the moment a real intrusion begins or a malicious action occurs and the moment a monitoring system or analyst first recognises it as such; Mean Time to Respond (MTTR, sometimes split into time to acknowledge, contain, eradicate and recover) measures the elapsed time from that detection to the point where the incident is contained or resolved. Both are averages over a population of alerts or incidents, so the underlying case definition matters more than the arithmetic: if you start the clock at ticket creation you measure your queue, not your detection. They are tracked operationally to expose where a SOC loses time, and they appear in board reporting and in service-level targets for managed detection providers. The usual mistake is treating a shrinking MTTD as proof of better security when the real change is a larger volume of low-severity alerts or a redefinition of when detection is declared; MTTR can likewise be gamed by closing tickets early. Neither metric describes coverage or dwell time on its own, so they belong alongside alert fidelity, escalation rate and true-positive ratio.

beginner.definition: Mean time to detect is the average time between two moments. The clock starts when a real security problem begins. It stops when your team first notices that problem. Mean time to respond is the average time from that moment until the problem is under control. The word mean simply means average. Both are measured in hours or days across many past incidents.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who is not noticed has time to steal data, add new accounts and hide again. If you never measure your detection speed, you cannot tell whether your monitoring is improving or getting worse. The same is true for response speed: a slow answer turns a small problem into a large one. These two numbers also help you explain to managers where the team loses time. Without them you can only guess, and guessing usually hides the real gap.
howItWorks: Something happens on the network, such as a strange login or a new program running on a server.
A tool records the event and sends a signal, which is called an alert, to the security team.
You note the time the event really started and the time you first understood it.
The gap between those two times is your detection time for that one case.
You do the same for response: from understanding the case to containing it.
Finally you average all the cases over a month to get one number for each measure.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk. A patient falls in a corridor at two in the morning. The time until a nurse finds the patient is like detection time. The time from finding the patient until a doctor arrives and the patient is safe is like response time. If the hospital counted only the second number, it would look fast. Yet patients could lie on the floor for an hour. Good managers watch both numbers, and they also ask how many falls were never noticed at all.
takeaways: Detection time measures how long a problem stays hidden, response time measures how long it stays uncontrolled.
Both are averages, so one very slow case can point to a broken process that the average hides.
Never compare these numbers between teams unless you know exactly when each team starts its clock.

objectives: Explain what mean time to detect and mean time to respond measure and what starts and stops each clock.
Describe how a security team collects the timestamps needed to calculate both metrics.
Identify common ways these numbers can be made to look better without real improvement.
Interpret a rising or falling detection time and suggest a plausible cause in a monitored environment.
Discuss how these metrics support incident reporting to managers without overstating security posture.
